results.name: new_set_first_trial_yes_gap
results.description: Yes rate on non-example targets on the first trial after the set changes (or session start, trial_index 0) minus yes rate on subsequent trials with the same set as the previous trial; nonzero observed vs a null near the stimulus-driven value means a set-novelty effect the stationary model lacks (positive = more liberal on the first query about a new set).
results.code:
# name: new_set_first_trial_yes_gap
# description: Yes rate on non-example targets on the first trial after the set changes (or session start, trial_index 0) minus yes rate on subsequent trials with the same set as the previous trial; nonzero observed vs a null near the stimulus-driven value means a set-novelty effect the stationary model lacks (positive = more liberal on the first query about a new set).
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    new = (s != s.shift(1)) | (df["trial_index"] == 0)
    ex = s.str.split(",")
    t = df["target"].astype(int).astype(str)
    isex = np.array([ti in e for ti, e in zip(t, ex)])
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    a = new.to_numpy() & ~isex
    b = (~new.to_numpy()) & ~isex
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: small_rule_nonmember_in_range_yes
results.description: Among sets of 2+ distinct examples that all fit some rule with <=20 members (squares, cubes, powers, multiples of 5-12, ends in d, ...), yes rate on non-example targets that are NOT in the smallest such rule and lie strictly between the smallest and largest example; observed below null means people reject rule-violating in-range targets more firmly than the model (its intervals/noise over-produce yes there), above null means people fill the range more.
results.code:
# name: small_rule_nonmember_in_range_yes
# description: Among sets of 2+ distinct examples that all fit some rule with <=20 members (squares, cubes, powers, multiples of 5-12, ends in d, ...), yes rate on non-example targets that are NOT in the smallest such rule and lie strictly between the smallest and largest example; observed below null means people reject rule-violating in-range targets more firmly than the model (its intervals/noise over-produce yes there), above null means people fill the range more.
def test_statistic(df):
    N = np.arange(1, 101)
    rules = [N % 2 == 1, N % 2 == 0, np.isin(N, [k * k for k in range(1, 11)]), np.isin(N, [1, 8, 27, 64]),
             np.isin(N, [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64]), np.isin(N, [3, 9, 27, 81]), np.isin(N, [4, 16, 64]),
             np.isin(N, [5, 25]), np.isin(N, [6, 36]), np.isin(N, [7, 49]), np.isin(N, [8, 64]), np.isin(N, [9, 81]),
             np.isin(N, [n for n in N if n > 1 and all(n % a for a in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1))])]
    rules += [N % m == 0 for m in range(3, 13)] + [N % 10 == d for d in range(10)]
    M = np.array(rules)
    size = M.sum(1)
    member = {}
    for s in df["number_set"].unique():
        ex = sorted(set(int(x) for x in str(s).split(",")))
        if len(ex) < 2:
            continue
        ok = M[:, np.array(ex) - 1].all(1)
        if not ok.any():
            continue
        r = np.where(ok)[0][np.argmin(size[ok])]
        if size[r] <= 20:
            member[s] = (M[r], ex[0], ex[-1], set(ex))
    if not member:
        return 0.0
    sub = df[df["number_set"].isin(list(member))]
    t = sub["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    sets = sub["number_set"].to_numpy()
    mem = np.array([member[s][0][ti - 1] for s, ti in zip(sets, t)])
    lo = np.array([member[s][1] for s in sets]); hi = np.array([member[s][2] for s in sets])
    isex = np.array([ti in member[s][3] for s, ti in zip(sets, t)])
    m = (~mem) & (~isex) & (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    return float(sub["rating"].to_numpy()[m].mean()) if m.any() else 0.0

results.name: single_example_divisor_multiple_bonus
results.description: For single-example sets with example >= 2, yes rate on non-example targets that divide or are a multiple of the example minus yes rate on other targets; observed above null means people use multiplicative (divisor/multiple) relations from one example more than the model (which lacks "divisors of n" concepts), below null means less.
results.code:
# name: single_example_divisor_multiple_bonus
# description: For single-example sets with example >= 2, yes rate on non-example targets that divide or are a multiple of the example minus yes rate on other targets; observed above null means people use multiplicative (divisor/multiple) relations from one example more than the model (which lacks "divisors of n" concepts), below null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    one = ~s.str.contains(",")
    sub = df[one]
    e = sub["number_set"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    t = sub["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = sub["rating"].to_numpy()
    keep = (e >= 2) & (t != e)
    rel = ((t % e == 0) | (e % t == 0)) & keep
    oth = (~((t % e == 0) | (e % t == 0))) & keep
    if not rel.any() or not oth.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[rel].mean() - r[oth].mean())

results.name: cell_unanimous_no_rate
results.description: Share of (set, target) cells (with >=5 responses) in which every response is "no"; observed above null means people reject more cells with total unanimity than the model's graded probabilities allow (the model spreads too much yes-probability over cells that people treat as clear non-members), below null the reverse.

results.name: ascending_order_generalization_gap
results.description: For sets of 3+ examples, yes rate on non-example targets when the examples were shown in ascending order minus when shown in non-ascending order; nonzero observed vs null means presentation order changes generalisation (positive = ordered sequences invite broader, rule-like generalisation), which the order-blind model can only produce through set content.
results.code:
# name: ascending_order_generalization_gap
# description: For sets of 3+ examples, yes rate on non-example targets when the examples were shown in ascending order minus when shown in non-ascending order; nonzero observed vs null means presentation order changes generalisation (positive = ordered sequences invite broader, rule-like generalisation), which the order-blind model can only produce through set content.
def test_statistic(df):
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    lists = s.str.split(",")
    n = lists.str.len().to_numpy()
    asc_map = {k: all(int(a) < int(b) for a, b in zip(k.split(",")[:-1], k.split(",")[1:])) for k in s.unique()}
    asc = s.map(asc_map).to_numpy().astype(bool)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).astype(str)
    isex = np.array([ti in e for ti, e in zip(t, lists)])
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy()
    a = (n >= 3) & asc & ~isex
    b = (n >= 3) & ~asc & ~isex
    if not a.any() or not b.any():
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: cell_unanimous_yes_rate
results.description: Share of (set, target) cells (with >=5 responses) in which every response is "yes"; observed above null means the model under-produces confident, unanimous endorsements (its yes-probabilities for clear members are too far below 1), below null means it over-produces them.
